claim: ARID1A is one of the most frequently mutated epigenetic regulators in a wide spectrum of cancers.
source: ARID1A is one of the most frequently mutated epigenetic regulators in a wide spectrum of cancers.
evidence: This is a general statement about ARID1A's mutation frequency across cancers, supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: ARID1A deficiency induces global changes in the epigenetic landscape of enhancers and promoters.
source: Recent studies have shown that ARID1A deficiency induces global changes in the epigenetic landscape of enhancers and promoters.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies mentioned in the abstract.

claim: ARID1A deficiency upregulates the expression of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 family member A1 (ALDH1A1) in a human cell line model.
source: In a human cell line model, we found that ARID1A deficiency upregulates the expression of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 family member A1 (ALDH1A1), which plays an essential role in attenuating the senescence induced by oncogenic KRAS through scavenging reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the human cell line model presented in the manuscript.

claim: ALDH1A1 plays an essential role in attenuating senescence induced by oncogenic KRAS through scavenging reactive oxygen species.
source: In a human cell line model, we found that ARID1A deficiency upregulates the expression of aldehyde dehydrogenase 1 family member A1 (ALDH1A1), which plays an essential role in attenuating the senescence induced by oncogenic KRAS through scavenging reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the mechanism of ALDH1A1 action.

claim: ARID1A deficiency increases the accessibility of the enhancer region of ALDH1A1.
source: As a subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex, our ATAC sequencing data showed that ARID1A deficiency increases the accessibility of the enhancer region of ALDH1A1.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ARID1A deficiency promotes pancreatic tumorigenesis by attenuating KRAS-induced senescence through the upregulation of ALDH1A1 expression.
source: This study provides the first evidence that ARID1A deficiency promotes pancreatic tumorigenesis by attenuating KRAS-induced senescence through the upregulation of ALDH1A1 expression.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) was the third leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States in 2018.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) was the third leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States in 2018 and is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related death by 2030 (Rahib et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rahib et al., 2014.

claim: PDAC is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related death by 2030.
source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) was the third leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States in 2018 and is projected to become the second leading cause of cancer-related death by 2030 (Rahib et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rahib et al., 2014.

claim: Clear driver mutations of PDAC include CDKN2A, TP53, SMAD4, and KRAS.
source: Besides the clear driver mutations of PDAC, which include CDKN2A, TP53, SMAD4, and KRAS, there are a large number of genes with low-frequency mutations (Waddell et al., 2015; Bailey et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: ARID1A has an 8% mutation rate in PDAC.
source: Among the genes with low-frequency mutations in PDAC, the top hit is ARID1A (a subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex) with an 8% mutation rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARID1A has a 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has an 18.7% mutation rate in gastric cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has an 18.6% mutation rate in bladder cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has a 13.7% mutation rate in hepatocellular cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has an 11.5% mutation rate in melanoma.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has a 9.4% mutation rate in colorectal cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has an 8.2% mutation rate in lung cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A has a 2.5% mutation rate in breast cancer.
source: In addition to PDAC, ARID1A is also frequently mutated in other cancer types, with 45.2% mutation rate in ovarian cancer, 18.7% in gastric cancer, 18.6% in bladder cancer, 13.7% in hepatocellular cancer, 11.5% in melanoma, 9.4% in colorectal cancer, 8.2% in lung cancer, and 2.5% in breast cancer (Kadoch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kadoch et al., 2013.

claim: ARID1A is involved in the regulation of differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis.
source: ARID1A is involved in the regulation of many biological processes of cells, including differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis (Wu and Roberts, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu and Roberts, 2013.

claim: ARID1A is necessary to maintain terminal differentiation of pancreatic acinar cells.
source: In pancreatic cancer, recent studies have shown that ARID1A is necessary to maintain terminal differentiation of pancreatic acinar cells, and knockout of ARID1A results in the accelerated formation of acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) and then pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) lesions (Zhang, 2018; Livshits et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang, 2018; Livshits et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: Knockout of ARID1A results in the accelerated formation of acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) and pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) lesions.
source: In pancreatic cancer, recent studies have shown that ARID1A is necessary to maintain terminal differentiation of pancreatic acinar cells, and knockout of ARID1A results in the accelerated formation of acinar-to-ductal metaplasia (ADM) and then pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) lesions (Zhang, 2018; Livshits et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zhang, 2018; Livshits et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019.

claim: ARID1A depletion can prime acinar cells for early-stage PanIN lesion formation by facilitating shifts in cell identity.
source: Although ARID1A depletion can prime acinar cells for early-stage PanIN lesion formation by facilitating shifts in cell identity (Livshits et al., 2018), the underlying mechanisms for the acceleration of ARID1A-deficiency-promoted PanIN progression remain elusive.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Livshits et al., 2018.

claim: ARID1A deficiency could facilitate intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) formation through MYC-mediated protein synthesis.
source: Besides PanIN lesions, ARID1A deficiency could also facilitate intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) formation through multiple pathways, including MYC-mediated protein synthesis (Wang et al., 2019) and SOX9/mTOR pathway (Kimura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claim: ARID1A deficiency could facilitate intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) formation through SOX9/mTOR pathway.
source: Besides PanIN lesions, ARID1A deficiency could also facilitate intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN) formation through multiple pathways, including MYC-mediated protein synthesis (Wang et al., 2019) and SOX9/mTOR pathway (Kimura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kimura et al., 2018.

claim: Arid1a knockout effectively reduces KRAS-induced senescence in PanIN lesions.
source: Our results showed that Arid1a knockout could effectively reduce KRAS-induced senescence in PanIN lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Cellular senescence is the major rate-limiting step in KRAS-driven PanIN progression.
source: It is important to point out that cellular senescence has been shown to be the major rate-limiting step in KRAS-driven PanIN progression (Morton et al., 2010; Serrano et al., 1997; Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morton et al., 2010; Serrano et al., 1997; Li et al., 2018.

claim: Aldehyde dehydrogenases play an essential role in attenuating senescence by scavenging reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by oncogenic KRAS.
source: Mechanistically, we found that aldehyde dehydrogenases play an essential role in attenuating senescence by scavenging the reactive oxygen species (ROS) induced by oncogenic KRAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Arid1a knockout facilitated the progression of lesions from ADM to PanIN3.
source: Consistent with the findings from other groups (Zhang, 2018; Livshits et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2019), we observed that Arid1a knockout facilitated the progression of lesions from ADM to PanIN3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C and citations to other studies.

claim: At the 2-month time point, the percentages of ADM, PanIN-1, and PanIN-2 were 74, 26, and 0%, respectively, in KC mice versus 53, 47, and 0% in AKC mice.
source: At as early as the 2-month time point, the percentages of ADM, PanIN-1, and PanIN-2 were 74, 26, and 0%, respectively, in KC mice versus 53, 47, and 0% in AKC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the study.

claim: At the 6-month time point, the percentages of ADM, PanIN-1, PanIN-2, and PanIN-3 were 77, 23, 0, and 0%, respectively, in KC mice versus 16, 74, 9, and 0.5% in AKC mice.
source: At the 6-month time point, the percentages of ADM, PanIN-1, PanIN-2, and PanIN-3 were 77, 23, 0, and 0%, respectively, in KC mice versus 16, 74, 9, and 0.5% in AKC mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: 20 lesions from two KC mice and 24 lesions from two AKC mice were profiled using MATQ-seq.
source: In total, we dissected and profiled 20 lesions from two KC mice and 24 lesions from two AKC mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size.

claim: 861 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between KC and AKC lesions, including 532 genes upregulated and 329 genes downregulated in AKC.
source: We observed that the lesions dissected from KC and AKC mice were clearly separated in the multidimensional scaling (MDS) plot, and 861 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Supplementary file 2), including 532 genes upregulated and 329 genes downregulated in AKC, were identified, which suggests the successful transcriptome profiling of individual PanIN lesions by MATQ-seq (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 25 gene sets were downregulated and two gene sets were upregulated in AKC lesions based on GSEA using Hallmark gene sets.
source: We observed that 25 gene sets were downregulated, and surprisingly, only two gene sets were upregulated in AKC lesions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Supplementary file 1, false discovery rate (FDR) < 0.1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The gene set KRAS_SIGNALING_UP was downregulated while the gene set KRAS_SIGNALING_DN was upregulated in AKC lesions.
source: The gene set KRAS_SIGNALING_UP was downregulated while the gene set KRAS_SIGNALING_DN was upregulated (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The activities of Kras signaling are partially impaired by Arid1a deficiency.
source: This observation suggests that the activities of Kras signaling are partially impaired by Arid1a deficiency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GSEA results.

claim: The Tp53 signaling pathway was suppressed in AKC lesions.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the Tp53 signaling pathway was suppressed in AKC lesions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ARID1A mutations are mutually exclusive with TP53 mutations in endometrial cancer.
source: ARID1A mutations have also been shown to be mutually exclusive with TP53 mutations in endometrial cancer (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2017.

claim: The senescence-associated signaling pathway is significantly suppressed in lesions from AKC mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that the senescence-associated signaling pathway is significantly suppressed in lesions from AKC mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The pathway activity associated with apoptosis was not significantly changed in AKC lesions.
source: In contrast, the pathway activity associated with apoptosis was not significantly changed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Multiple signaling pathways associated with inflammation, including TNFα signaling, IL6–STAT3 signaling, IL2–STAT5 signaling, IFN-α signaling, and IFN-γ signaling, were significantly suppressed in Arid1a KO lesions.
source: Indeed, we observed that multiple signaling pathways associated with inflammation, including TNFα signaling, IL6–STAT3 signaling, IL2–STAT5 signaling, IFN-α signaling, and IFN-γ signaling, were significantly suppressed in Arid1a KO lesions (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: SA-β-Gal-positive lesions were observed in five out of seven (71%) KC mice.
source: SA-β-Gal-positive lesions were observed in five out of seven (71%) KC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by SA-β-Gal staining data.

claim: Only one out of six (17%) AKC mice showed SA-β-Gal-positive lesions.
source: In contrast, only one out of six (17%) AKC mice showed SA-β-Gal-positive lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by SA-β-Gal staining data.

claim: The percentage of SA-β-Gal-positive lesions in KC mice was about twice that in AKC mice.
source: Among the mice with SA-β-Gal-positive lesions, the percentage of SA-β-Gal-positive lesions in KC mice was about twice of that in AKC mice (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The intensity of SA-β-Gal staining in acinar cells from AKC mice was significantly less than that from KC mice in ex vivo culture.
source: We observed that the intensity of SA-β-Gal staining in acinar cells from AKC mice was significantly less than that from KC mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by ex vivo culture data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: The effect of Arid1a knockout on senescence is likely an intrinsic cellular response rather than a microenvironmental response.
source: Importantly, this result suggests that the effect of Arid1a knockout on senescence is likely an intrinsic cellular response rather than a microenvironmental response such as accelerated clearance of senescent cells by immune cells (Pignolo et al., 2020; Baker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the ex vivo culture results, supported by citations.

claim: Knockout of ARID1A drastically increased the number of cells escaping from KRAS-induced senescence in colony formation assay.
source: We observed that knockout of ARID1A drastically increased the number of cells escaping from KRAS-induced senescence (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The gene set KRAS_SIGNALING_UP was downregulated in ARID1A-KO cells compared with wildtype cells.
source: Interestingly, we found the gene set KRAS_SIGNALING_UP was downregulated in ARID1A-KO cells compared with wildtype cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), which is consistent with our data from PanIN lesions.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The phosphorylation of ERK upon KRAS induction in ARID1A-KO cells was significantly reduced in comparison with the wildtype cells.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, the phosphorylation of ERK upon KRAS induction in ARID1A-KO cells was significantly reduced in comparison with the wildtype cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Four out of six signaling pathways remarkably repressed in ARID1A-KO HPNE cells are involved in inflammatory response.
source: GSEA results showed that six signaling pathways were remarkably repressed in ARID1A-KO HPNE cells, and four of them are involved in inflammatory response (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B), which is consistent with what we observed in PanIN lesions from AKC mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: The activation of CDKN1A expression upon KRAS induction was significantly reduced in the ARID1A-KO cell line.
source: We observed that the activation of CDKN1A expression upon KRAS induction was also significantly reduced in the ARID1A-KO cell line (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D), which indicates that our HPNE cell line model successfully recapitulated the senescence phenotypes observed in the mouse model.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: 125 genes were upregulated and 165 genes were downregulated between wildtype and ARID1A-KO cells with KRAS induction.
source: For the first clone with KRAS induction, we identified 125 upregulated genes and 165 downregulated genes between the wildtype and the ARID1A-KO line (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 57 out of 125 upregulated genes (46%) are shared between conditions with or without KRAS induction.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, for the upregulated genes, 57 out of 125 genes (46%) are shared between the two conditions and the expected number of random overlap is 1.79.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 54 out of 165 downregulated genes (33%) are shared between conditions with or without KRAS induction.
source: For the downregulated genes, 54 out of 165 genes (33%) are shared and the expected number of random overlap is 3.38.
evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ALDH1A1 exhibits significant change in differential gene expression for both conditions: with or without KRAS induction.
source: Among the DEGs between ARID1A-KO and wildtype HPNE cells, ALDH1A1 exhibits the significant change in differential gene expression for both conditions: with or without KRAS induction (Figure 3B and D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B and D.

claim: ALDH1A1 has been shown to participate in the clearance of ROS.
source: Considering that ALDH1A1 has been shown to participate in the clearance of ROS (Raha et al., 2014) and ROS are vital mediators of KRAS-induced senescence (Storz, 2017), we hypothesize that ALDH1A1 is the gene that mediates the effect of ARID1A deficiency on KRAS-induced senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Raha et al., 2014.

claim: ROS are vital mediators of KRAS-induced senescence.
source: Considering that ALDH1A1 has been shown to participate in the clearance of ROS (Raha et al., 2014) and ROS are vital mediators of KRAS-induced senescence (Storz, 2017), we hypothesize that ALDH1A1 is the gene that mediates the effect of ARID1A deficiency on KRAS-induced senescence.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Storz, 2017.

claim: Aldh3a1 is significantly upregulated in lesions from AKC mice.
source: Interestingly, we observed that Aldh3a1 is significantly upregulated in lesions from AKC mice (Figure 3F and Supplementary file 2), which was further confirmed by immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by PanIN-seq data shown in Figure 3F and IHC data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: In different species different types of ALDH family proteins can be used to mediate the attenuation of Kras-induced senescence in Arid1a-deficient cells.
source: This result suggests that in different species different types of ALDH family proteins can be used to mediate the attenuation of Kras-induced senescence in Arid1a-deficient cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ALDH1A1 is upregulated in human cells while Aldh3a1 is upregulated in mouse cells.

claim: In 63% of PDAC samples, the expression levels of ALDH1A1 are higher than 50 TPM.
source: In contrast to the expression levels in normal ductal cells, we observed that in 63% of PDAC samples, the expression levels of ALDH1A1 are higher than 50 TPM, and in 10% of samples, the expression levels are higher than 200 TPM (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PDAC expression data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In 10% of PDAC samples, the expression levels of ALDH1A1 are higher than 200 TPM.
source: In contrast to the expression levels in normal ductal cells, we observed that in 63% of PDAC samples, the expression levels of ALDH1A1 are higher than 50 TPM, and in 10% of samples, the expression levels are higher than 200 TPM (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of PDAC expression data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Only 0.2% of PDAC patients (1 out of 576 patient samples from two cohorts) acquired mutations in ALDH1A1.
source: We observed that only 0.2% of the patients (1 out of 576 patient samples from two cohorts [Bailey et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017]) acquired mutations in ALDH1A1 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutation analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Inhibition of ALDH1A1 activity significantly decreased the number of colonies formed in ARID1A knockout cells.
source: We observed that inhibition of ALDH1A1 activity significantly decreased the number of colonies formed in ARID1A knockout cells; in contrast, no significant changes were observed in the wildtype cells (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by colony formation assay data with DEAB treatment shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The colony number in ARID1A-KO cells with ALDH1A1 knockdown was significantly less than that without ALDH1A1 knockdown.
source: We also observed that the colony number in ARID1A-KO cells with ALDH1A1 knockdown was significantly less than that without ALDH1A1 knockdown (Figure 4E,F), which is consistent with the results of the ALDH inhibitor experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by colony formation assay data with ALDH1A1 knockdown shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: The fraction of ROS-positive cells in ARID1A-KO iKRAS-HPNE cells was significantly less than in wildtype cells, regardless of KRAS induction.
source: We observed that the fraction of ROS-positive cells in ARID1A-KO iKRAS-HPNE cells was significantly less than in wildtype cells, regardless of KRAS induction (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The ROS level in ALDH1A1 knockdown cells was significantly higher than that observed in the cells with scramble shRNA.
source: We observed that the ROS level in ALDH1A1 knockdown cells was significantly higher than that observed in the cells with scramble shRNA (Figure 4H), indicating that ALDH1A1 is responsible for the clearance of ROS in HPNE cells with ARID1A knockout.
evidence: This claim is supported by ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: ALDH1A1 is responsible for the clearance of ROS in HPNE cells with ARID1A knockout.
source: We observed that the ROS level in ALDH1A1 knockdown cells was significantly higher than that observed in the cells with scramble shRNA (Figure 4H), indicating that ALDH1A1 is responsible for the clearance of ROS in HPNE cells with ARID1A knockout.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ROS measurement data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: ARID1A knockout can effectively reduce cellular ROS levels by upregulating the expression of ALDH1A1, which leads to significant attenuation of KRAS-induced senescence and acceleration of PanIN progression.
source: From the results above, we conclude that ARID1A knockout can effectively reduce cellular ROS levels by upregulating the expression of ALDH1A1, which then leads to significant attenuation of KRAS-induced senescence and acceleration of PanIN progression (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence and illustrated in Figure 4I.

claim: The Spearman correlation coefficients between knockout and wildtype cells are significantly lower than those between replicate samples in both groups.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the Spearman correlation coefficients between knockout and wildtype cells are significantly lower than those between replicate samples in both groups (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that the changes in DNA accessibility were robustly captured.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: The number of peaks affected by ARID1A deficiency in the distal regulatory regions is significantly larger than the number of peaks in promoter regions.
source: We plotted a scatter plot of read counts in peaks between wildtype and ARID1A-KO for promoters (Figure 5C) and enhancers (Figure 5D) and observed that the number of peaks affected by ARID1A deficiency in the distal regulatory regions is significantly larger than the number of peaks in promoter regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: ARID1A knockout alters gene expression mainly by modulating the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer elements.
source: This result further supports that ARID1A knockout alters gene expression mainly by modulating the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer elements.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data showing more changes in enhancer regions than promoter regions.

claim: Chromatin accessibility decreased in ARID1A-KO cells compared to wildtype cells for genes involved in KRAS signaling.
source: We observed that in comparison to the wildtype cells, chromatin accessibility decreased in ARID1A-KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: AR1D1A deficiency impairs the activities of the KRAS signaling pathways by partially impairing the chromatin accessibility of the genes downstream of the KRAS pathways.
source: This observation suggests that AR1D1A deficiency impairs the activities of the KRAS signaling pathways by partially impairing the chromatin accessibility of the genes downstream of the KRAS pathways.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ATAC-seq data for KRAS signaling genes.

claim: The binding motifs of SRY, FOX family, CDX1, SOX5, etc., were enriched in the ATAC peaks with significantly increased accessibility in ARID1A-KO cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that the binding motifs of SRY, FOX family, CDX1, SOX5, etc., were enriched in the ATAC peaks with significantly increased accessibility in ARID1A-KO cells (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 6A,B and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The binding motifs of the FOS-JUN family, NFE2, NF2L1, etc., were significantly enriched in the ATAC peaks with significantly decreased accessibility.
source: The binding motifs of the FOS-JUN family, NFE2, NF2L1, etc., were significantly enriched in the ATAC peaks with significantly decreased accessibility (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 6B, and Supplementary file 7), which is consistent with the results of a recent study showing ARID1A as a co-factor of AP-1 (Sen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5G and a citation to Sen et al., 2019.

claim: There was a significant increase in accessibility in 9 out of 11 peaks at the distal regions of ALDH1A1 when comparing ARID1A-KO cells with wildtype cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that there was a significant increase in accessibility in 9 out of 11 peaks at the distal regions when we compared ARID1A-KO cells with wildtype cells (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data for ALDH1A1 locus.

claim: Five enhancer loci of ALDH1A1 clearly overlapped with the active enhancer markers H3K27ac and H3K4me1.
source: We observed that five enhancer loci clearly overlapped with the active enhancer markers (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of ATAC-seq peaks with ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A consistent increase in accessibility was observed in ARID1A knockout cells in comparison with wildtype cells for the five enhancer loci of ALDH1A1.
source: For the five enhancer loci, we observed a consistent increase in accessibility in ARID1A knockout cells in comparison with wildtype cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ARID1A deficiency upregulates ALDH1A1 expression by increasing the accessibility of the associated enhancer elements.
source: Overall, these results confirm that ARID1A deficiency upregulates ALDH1A1 expression by increasing the accessibility of the associated enhancer elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATAC-seq data for ALDH1A1 enhancers.

claim: Both EP300 and NR3C1 knockdowns could significantly impair the transcription of the ALDH1A1 gene.
source: In Figure 6C (middle and right panels), we observed that both knockdowns could significantly impair the transcription of the ALDH1A1 gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ARID1A deficiency promotes active transcription of ALDH1A1 by altering genome accessibility and allowing the binding of EP300 and/or NR3C1 to the corresponding enhancer loci.
source: Collectively, these data also indicate that ARID1A deficiency promotes active transcription of ALDH1A1 by altering genome accessibility and therefore allowing the binding of EP300 and/or NR3C1 to the corresponding enhancer loci.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ATAC-seq and knockdown experiments.

claim: KRAS can upregulate the expression of multiple oxidoreductases via NRF2 to counteract oncogenic stress.
source: It has been shown that KRAS can upregulate the expression of multiple oxidoreductases via NRF2 (nuclear factor, erythroid derived 2, like 2) to counteract oncogenic stress (DeNicola et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to DeNicola et al., 2011.

claim: KRAS can enhance NADPH production by reprogramming the metabolism of glutamine to assist oxidoreductases in scavenging ROS.
source: Meanwhile, KRAS can also enhance NADPH production by reprogramming the metabolism of glutamine to assist oxidoreductases in scavenging ROS (Son et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Son et al., 2013.

claim: A high percentage of senescent PanIN lesions occur in the pancreas of KC mice.
source: However, the observation that a high percentage of senescent PanIN lesions occur in the pancreas of KC mice suggests that the mechanisms described above likely have limited effects in reducing Kras-induced ROS in neoplastic lesions.
evidence: This is an observation from the study that supports the inference about limited effects of existing mechanisms.

claim: ARID1A has been linked to the regulation of ROS through other pathways in different cancer types.
source: It is worth noting that ARID1A has also been linked to the regulation of ROS through other pathways.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to other studies.

claim: ARID1A overexpression causes an increase in ROS by activating transcription of cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP450) at the initiation stage of liver cancer.
source: Sun et al. found that ARID1A overexpression causes an increase in ROS by activating transcription of cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP450) at the initiation stage of liver cancer (Sun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2017.

claim: ARID1A deficiency results in elevated ROS by inhibiting the transcription of SLC7A11 in ovarian cancer.
source: Interestingly, Ogiwara et al. found that ARID1A deficiency results in elevated ROS by inhibiting the transcription of SLC7A11 (a transporter gene required for the import of cystine and the production of glutathione) in ovarian cancer (Ogiwara et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ogiwara et al., 2019.

claim: The effects of ARID1A deficiency on ROS are likely tissue-specific.
source: Therefore, the effects of ARID1A deficiency on ROS are likely tissue-specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on the different effects of ARID1A on ROS in different cancer types.

claim: ARID1A deficiency directly suppresses the activities of KRAS signaling.
source: Besides reducing ROS levels through the upregulation of ALDH family proteins, we also observed that ARID1A deficiency directly suppresses the activities of KRAS signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Both reduction of KRAS activities and inflammatory cytokine response are consistent with increased attenuation of Kras-induced senescence upon ARID1A knockout.
source: Both reduction of KRAS activities and inflammatory cytokine response are also consistent with our observation of the increased attenuation of Kras-induced senescence upon ARID1A knockout.
evidence: This is an inference connecting multiple observations from the study.

claim: Mutant KRAS signaling needs to be tuned to efficiently drive tumorigenesis: too much signaling could lead to cell growth arrest, while too little signaling could limit proliferation.
source: Overall, experimental evidence shows that mutant KRAS signaling needs to be tuned to efficiently drive tumorigenesis: too much signaling could lead to cell growth arrest, while too little signaling could limit proliferation (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: KRAS could harness its own activities by changing the mutation pattern and seeking cooperation with other genes through passive selection during tumor development.
source: To find the 'sweet spot' of KRAS activation, KRAS could harness its own activities by changing the mutation pattern (including mutation position and type of substitution) and seeking cooperation with other genes (e.g., mutagenesis of tumor suppressors) through the course of passive selection during tumor development (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: This study demonstrates the important roles of epigenetic mutations in harnessing KRAS activities and promoting tumorigenesis.
source: Overall, our study demonstrates the important roles of epigenetic mutations in harnessing KRAS activities and promoting tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.
